title: The Concord circle
hook: Emerson gathered Thoreau, Margaret Fuller and others in a small town

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was hitch your wagon to a star: aim your work at the great forces, and let them pull. Your line was hitch it to a star.

A small town in Massachusetts. A river, a few roads, a green, a white church, farms running out toward the woods. Concord. Nothing on a map would suggest anything unusual. But for a stretch of years, the people walking its roads and knocking on each other's doors included Emerson, a young surveyor and pencil-maker named Henry David Thoreau, and visitors like the writer and editor Margaret Fuller. They argued, borrowed books, took long walks, and read each other's drafts.
screen: `A SMALL TOWN, A RIVER, A GREEN.` → `EMERSON, THOREAU, FULLER.` → `WALKS, ARGUMENTS, DRAFTS.`

segments.voice: First, very different people. They didn't always agree. Emerson gave lectures and wrote essays for a wide public. Thoreau went off to live by a pond. Fuller, an editor and critic, pressed her own questions hard, and tomorrow is hers. What held them together wasn't a shared program; it was the habit of thinking out loud with each other. Second, an honest portrait. When Thoreau died, Emerson spoke about him without sanding off the odd edges: "He was bred to no profession; he never married; he lived alone; he never went to church; he never voted." Not a list of complaints. A friend loved exactly as he was, sincere to the end, the test from Friendship last week. Third, a story people tell. When Thoreau spent a night in jail for refusing to pay a tax, the story goes, Emerson came by and asked why he was in there, and Thoreau asked why Emerson was out there. It probably didn't happen in those words. It's told because it captures a real friendship: two people who could challenge each other and stay close. Fourth, the week in a circle: grief that taught nothing, the years that teach, the poet who names, the poem from his reading of the east, the best day, the wagon and the star. Emerson wrote at his own desk, but he lived among friends who read his drafts and argued back.

segments.voice: Let two people come to mind, friends you can think out loud with, or would like to; maybe they've never met. Picture the three of you together, on a walk, at a meal, around a table with coffee, and the question or book you'd want to talk about. Notice how it feels to sit in the middle of that circle.
